results_so_far.title: Chunk 3: ECMP baseline, and a move onto a loaded path helps the mover and hurts the bystander
results_so_far.verdict: Finish line met · two findings change the method
results_so_far.summary: ECMP with OpenFlow 1.3 select groups now runs through a reusable, seeded runner (10 seeds, 30 s each, 4 elephants and about 1050 mice per run). Hash collisions decide everything: an elephant alone on its uplink gets 8.70 Mbit/s, two sharing get 4.42 each, three get 3.09. Mice complete in 50.8 ms at the median but 1210 ms at p99, mostly lost handshakes. Then a deliberate move of elephant E0 from a slow spine onto a fast spine already carrying elephant B gave the opposite of the pre-registered prediction: E0 gained 13% over a no-gap move, B lost 17%, and total goodput on the shared path barely changed. Along the way the runner caught an emulation artifact (TCP Small Queues counting the emulated switch queue) that, left in place, flips that result to a 47% loss for the moved flow.

rows: Elephant goodput by elephants sharing its uplink (1 / 2 / 3)
Elephant goodput per run, mean of 4 / worst of 4
Mice flow completion time, p50 / p99
50.8 ± 5.8 / 1210 ± 100 ms (p99 is mostly 1 s SYN timeouts, 2.3% of mice)
2596 / 2617 / 2657 / 2662, chi-square p = 0.76; no flow ever changed spine
same schedule hash, same spine for 3169 / 3169 flows
Loaded move, moved flow E0: slow→fast (9 ms gap) vs fast→fast, 10 s window
Loaded move, bystander B: slow→fast vs no move, 10 s window
Loaded move, E0 + B total: slow→fast vs no move
Same move with the old host queue setting (TSQ artifact present)

notes: Methods finding: in Mininet, packets sitting in the emulated switch queue stay charged to the sending socket, so TCP Small Queues caps each flow at a few packets in the switch. The bottleneck never fills, there is almost no loss, and cwnd stops deciding the rate (packets out / cwnd 0.5 to 0.67, 27 drops in 10 s). A 10 µs netem qdisc on every host NIC frees the packet as it leaves the host, like a real NIC (packets out / cwnd 1.00, 118 drops). Every run from Chunk 3 on uses it; Chunk 2 stays as recorded.

Why the sign flipped: E0 arrives from the 10 ms path with a larger cwnd (25 vs 19 segments) and keeps a larger one afterwards, so it takes share from B. Reordering still happens (events in 9 of 10 runs) and cwnd is still cut (25 to 8), but the cut lands on a flow that starts ahead. This is an inference from the counters, not a tested mechanism.

Damage is now defined with three terms, from Chunk 4 on: the moved flow’s deficit, the deficit of the flows already on the destination path, and the total goodput lost on that path, each against its matched no-move control. The moved-flow-only number stays as a reported column to show why it fails under load.

Max link utilisation is 1.0 in every ECMP run, so it will not separate controllers; elephant goodput and mice FCT will. Every number here was recomputed from the raw data by an independent agent with its own code and confirmed.
results_so_far.source: STATUS.md and LOG.md (Chunk 3 sections) on main; raw data in results/ecmp/, results/loaded/ and results/tsq/.

results_so_far.title: Chunk 2: a reroute does measurable damage, and it is small on an idle path
results_so_far.summary: A single 10 Mbit/s TCP flow was moved between spines once, with one OFPFC_MODIFY_STRICT on the ingress leaf, and watched for 2 s after the flow-mod’s barrier reply. Every slow-to-fast move produced reordering and spurious retransmissions; no control did. The goodput lost in those 2 s was 0.29% at a 4 ms delay gap and 2.81% at a 9 ms gap. The cause is the one the proposal predicted: packets on the new, faster path overtake packets still on the old one, the sender retransmits segments that were never lost, and cwnd is cut. In all 80 trials the kernel never undid that cut. With one flow on an idle path the cut costs almost nothing, which is the caveat. Chunk 3 tests the same mechanism with competing flows.

columns: Goodput deficit in 2 s vs control
rows: no reroute (controls on 1, 5 and 10 ms spines)

notes: Retransmissions after a move are almost all spurious: the retransmitted-segment count matches the DSACK count in every reroute condition (R1 5.2 vs 5.0, R2 8.6 vs 6.3, R0 5.2 vs 5.2, R3 3.0 vs 3.0 per move).
R2’s deficit is dominated by 3 of 10 trials that hit a retransmission timeout; the other 7 lose 10.8 KB each (post-hoc table in verdict.md, not part of the verdict).
Steady goodput before every move was 9.564 Mbit/s of 10. Flow-mod to barrier reply took a median of 1.15 ms, so the move itself drops nothing; the damage is TCP behaviour.
A second run of R2 and C1 as root on the system Open vSwitch agreed with the rootless campaign.
